newsitem.title: UK: Norway crown settles after rescue by central bank.
newsitem.headline: Norway crown settles after rescue by central bank.

text.p: Norway's central bank threw its ailing currency a lifeline by saying it would step into the forex market when necessary, reversing a policy of non-intervention it had kept since January.
The Norges Bank's announcement on Tuesday stemmed a freefall that started on Monday in the Norwegian crown, which dropped to its lowest level against the mark since October 25.

"It was a commitment to intervene in the market again to prevent the central bank from having to hike rates if the crown weakens further from here," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The crown had been softening recently due to a rise in inflation, weaker oil prices and worries about Norway's political scene before parliamentary elections in September.

This week's accelerated drop in the crown, a currency known for its volatility, was triggered by heavy selling from corporations and U.S. funds in a move apparently unrelated to fundamentals, traders said.
The crown fell to a seven-month low of 4.2400 per mark earlier on Tuesday, compared with 4.2260/90 in late European trade on Monday.

But it bounced back when the Norges Bank said it no longer found it necessary to keep its self-imposed limits on managing the crown's exchange rate. The central bank has a policy of intervening to maintain an unannounced target.

"The market was looking at the crown on the Ecu index, which was up at around 104, which was quite weak. And people sold mark/Norway on the expectation they (the Norges Bank) would try to get the index back down close to 100," said a trader at a Scandinavian bank.

The crown was at 103.95 against the inverse European Currency Unit index in early trade. The index is a theoretical basket used by the central bank to monitor the unit. The lower the figure, the stronger the crown is relative to the basket.
The central bank's policy change was not likely to push the crown up strongly, but it would help keep the unit from moving at breakneck speed, analysts said.

"It's mildly positive for the crown...Basically, it means the central bank will be using exchange rates more to control growth and inflation problems which may be emerging, not interest rates," Lewis said.
Higher-than-expected consumer prices announced earlier this month had stoked fears of rising inflation, drawing attention to the fact that the weakening crown could exacerbate this problem.
"The risk that Norway could import inflation (due to the crown's weakness) became overwhelming, and they had to stop the currency," said Claudio Demolli, foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch.

Analysts said the crown would now likely settle around 4.10-4.20 to the mark, its range since mid-April, with help from the market's nervousness over European economic and monetary union (EMU). Norway is not linked to the single currency project.

"The crown isn't really big enough or steady enough to become a safe-haven currency. At the same time, it's shielded from the noise about EMU, which will continue among the other European currencies for the next year or so," Demolli said.
